newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cattle group urges changes in CME futures.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cattle group urges changes in CME futures.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange live cattle futures contract needs changes to improve its relation to cash basis markets if it is to grow as a hedging tool, the National Cattlemen's Beef Association said.

"Many legitimate hedgers of fed cattle have complained that the current contract is not a viable risk management tool because of basis unpredictability," Paul Hitch, chairman of NCBA's Live Cattle Marketing Committee, said in a statement.
The statement, released by NCBA on Tuesday, summarized Hitch's testimony on February 20 before the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which is reviewing the cattle contract.
The CFTC is currently weighing approval of changes proposed by the CME for the live cattle contract.

The changes include modifying yield/grade specifications and calculations for non-par price differentials; extending the period for live-graded cattle deliveries by five days; changing the last trading day for expiring contracts; and raising speculative position limits during delivery.
Hitch said NCBA recommended that the CFTC reject the proposed increase in speculative position limits until the revised contract has traded for at least one year.
CME has proposed raising speculative position limits on the spot month cattle contract to 600 contracts from 300 except during the last five trading days of the expiring contract month.
"We are unwilling to have our members, legitimate hedgers, be exposed to additional speculative risk until there is evidence the contract has improved basis predictability," Hitch said.
NCBA said the U.S. Agriculture Department's Market News report "National Premiums and Discounts" should be based on weighted averages and actual market transactions in order to ensure its usefulness.

The USDA report, issued on Mondays, currently presents value adjustments for quality, yield grade and weights on beef carcasses that are designed as benchmark differentials to aid delivery of carcasses against the existing CME contract.
"NCBA also urges CFTC to develop an interagency initiative with the USDA to assure the report is free from potential manipulation and has integrity throughout the beef industry," the statement said.
NCBA asked CFTC to allow heifers for delivery against the CME contract, which currently allows only steers. NCBA said heifers now account for 38 percent of U.S. slaughter cattle.
NCBA also told CFTC it was studying the possibility of adding a cash settlement option for CME cattle deliveries and had set up a working group to give a recommendation.
"If the working group reaches a clear consensus in favor of cash settlement, NCBA urges CME to withdraw the current proposal and submit a proposal for cash settlement," it said.
